assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a new regime of light-matter interaction in a solid-state device: strong coupling of a single artificial atom to a single microwave photon, with dispersive readout and controllable coupling. It is the architecture on which most present superconducting quantum processors rest, and it also created microwave quantum optics on a chip. The discovery is a clean, controllable demonstration of basic quantum physics, and it is the physics that makes the platform possible, not merely an engineering application. I rank it first on the merits of the field, while declaring that it is close to my own research area and that I should be careful not to overweight familiarity.
assessment.attribution: Blais supplied the 2004 theoretical proposal with Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf. Wallraff and Schoelkopf led the 2004 Nature experiment demonstrating strong coupling, and each then built a major experimental program on it. The three credited names give a coherent theory plus two experimental leaders configuration. The decisive roles of Girvin and Majer, Devoret and others in the early Yale work are not in the credited list, so the allocation is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Mature. More than twenty years of independent confirmation across many laboratories, with reproducible device physics and wide adoption in quantum computing and quantum optics. Recognition is timely, with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits having now covered the neighbouring foundation.
uncertainties: The committee may feel that superconducting circuits were recognised in 2025 and not want to return to the area so soon.
Credit boundaries with the Yale group (Girvin, Majer, Devoret, Huang) are contested and the credited names exclude some of them.
My proximity to the field and to WACQT is a potential conflict of interest that the committee should weigh.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock, which removes motional and light-shift errors, and Ye realised strontium lattice clocks with many atoms and reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The advance is a real step in precision measurement, makes new tests of fundamental physics possible, and is a clear, original idea followed by a rigorous experimental realisation. It sits well with earlier clock and frequency-comb prizes without duplicating them.
assessment.attribution: Katori is the clear inventor of the lattice-clock concept (2001-2003), and Ye is the leading realiser who pushed it to record accuracy. The two-person configuration is clean. Others (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) made important contributions, but the idea and the decisive realisation are well captured by these two.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Multiple independent laboratories operate lattice clocks and compare them at the 1e-18 level, and the redefinition of the second is being discussed. Recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the clock as adding enough beyond the existing prizes on laser cooling, frequency combs and ion clocks.
The extent of the contribution of other groups and of ion-clock competitors to the accuracy record.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental observation of the Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed the mechanism recognised in 2013 and completed the Standard Model. It is a landmark in originality of scale and in clarity of result, with two independent experiments reaching five sigma and then measuring properties. I defer to colleagues in particle physics for the finer judgement, but the importance is not in doubt.
assessment.attribution: The principal difficulty is that a discovery by two collaborations of several thousand people cannot be assigned to three individuals without arbitrary choices. Jenni and Della Negra founded and led ATLAS and CMS proposals, and Gianotti led ATLAS at the time of discovery; Virdee is an equally credible CMS choice, and the CMS spokesperson at discovery is not in the list. I take one ATLAS leader and the two founders, and flag that this is a judgement the particle physicists should lead. The statutes also limit the number of laureates, and a collaboration prize is not allowed.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with a decade of precision coupling measurements by both experiments. Recognition is somewhat overdue given the 2013 theory prize.
uncertainties: No fair three-person allocation exists for two very large collaborations, and my chosen subset is open to challenge.
My own expertise outside quantum optics and superconducting devices is limited, so I give the particle physics experts' view priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator introduced a new class of matter classified by topology and spin-orbit coupling, and Kane and Mele's theory was followed by an experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells with edge conductance quantised at the predicted value. It extends the topological ideas recognised in 2016 and led to a large field. The experimental confirmation is crisp and quantitative.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the 2005 theoretical proposals, and Molenkamp's group (with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's HgTe prediction) provided the 2007 experiment. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu, Kane (3D) are not in the credited names, and the contribution of Zhang (deceased) and Bernevig is the principal unresolved allocation. Within the given names the theory plus experiment trio is reasonable.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Edge transport has been reproduced, and the 3D topological insulators were confirmed by ARPES and transport by many groups. Recognition is timely, with some risk that the topological phase of matter of 2016 is felt to cover this ground.
uncertainties: The role of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang in predicting the HgTe realisation, which is not in the credited list.
Whether the committee sees the field as sufficiently distinct from the 2016 topological-phase prize.
The relation to B014, which covers the same field with a different candidate set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene, and Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulators and superconductivity there in 2018. This opened a very large field of tunable moiré quantum matter, with correlated physics controlled by a gate voltage. The prediction followed by experiment pattern is the sort of discovery the prize rewards.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) and the experimental discovery (Cao, Jarillo-Herrero 2018) form a natural split. The experimental credit is arguably shared with Cory Dean and the Columbia/other groups on hBN-based moiré devices, and Yuan Cao, as first author, did not make the list.
assessment.maturity: Fairly young, about eight years since the experiments. Reproducibility of superconductivity and correlated states across groups is good, but the nature of the superconductivity and the mechanisms remain debated, so recognition may still be somewhat early.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism and the full phase diagram are not settled.
Credit among the Jarillo-Herrero, Dean, Kim and Young groups and the theorists is not fully resolved.
Sample-to-sample variation (twist-angle disorder) was a concern in early work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with controllable parameters, shown by the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later by single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes. It is a clean quantum simulator of many-body physics in which the Hamiltonian is known. The importance is clear, though the answers to open condensed-matter questions are still incomplete.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, and Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott insulator experiment (with Hänsch's group), and Bloch and Greiner led the microscope work. Esslinger's fermionic Mott insulator is also a decisive experiment and the credit among four people cannot be reduced to three without a loss.
assessment.maturity: Mature in technique with many replicating laboratories, while the scientific payoffs for open problems such as the doped Hubbard model are still developing.
uncertainties: Excluding Esslinger and Jaksch is an arbitrary cut.
Overlap with B055 and B052 for Zoller and Cirac, and with the earlier 2001 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the simulation has yet delivered a result that one could not obtain otherwise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Caves proposed squeezed light to beat the standard quantum limit in interferometers, Kimble made the first experimental squeezed state by four-wave mixing, and squeezing is now routinely used in the gravitational-wave detectors. It is a basic quantum optical phenomenon turned into a working improvement in a major instrument. The importance is high, although the detector application is one step removed from the 2017 prize.
assessment.attribution: Caves for the theory and the interferometer proposal, Kimble and Slusher et al. for the first experiments, and Schnabel for the demonstration at GEO600 and later work. Mavalvala and the LIGO squeezing team are in the credited list and arguably decisive for the application. The group of experimentalists who first made squeezed light (Slusher, Wu, Kimble) is not fully captured.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense that squeezing is deployed in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 and the benefit is measured. The long gap between theory and experiments blurs the question of who did the original discovery.
uncertainties: Different parts of the discovery (generation, theory, application) may need different recognition.
Candidate B041 overlaps strongly, and the committee would have to choose one framing.
Slusher and Walls, who are important for the first experiments and theory, are not credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of quantised conductance in steps of 2e^2/h in a ballistic point contact is a very clear, beautiful demonstration of Landauer transport in a controllable mesoscopic device, and it is the base for quantum point contacts used throughout quantum-dot and spin-qubit work. It is related to my early field of mesoscopic transport, so I may be biased. The physics is elegant, but one might judge it as a step in a field rather than a new regime of physics.
assessment.attribution: Two groups, van Wees (Delft/Philips) and Wharam, Pepper et al. (Cambridge), published independently and almost simultaneously in 1988. The credit is naturally split between them, and the credited pair fits. Other contributors, such as Thornton, Ritchie, and Landauer for the theoretical concept, are not included, so the allocation is not entirely clean.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, now more than 35 years old and reproduced in countless devices. Recognition is probably late, with a risk that the discovery is seen as a precursor to prizes already given on the quantum Hall effect.
uncertainties: Whether the committee thinks the result is enough for a prize on its own rather than as part of the broader mesoscopic field.
Credit among the two experimental groups and the theoretical precursors (Landauer, Büttiker).
My own background may bias me towards this candidate.
